The reasons why I dont think this statement is true is because it is not that welfare and peace flow out any democracy, but instead democracy is a consequence from or necessarily needs what it further perpetuates: peace and welfare - in that order. The past decade in the Middle-East remind me of medieval europe in that there was competitive souvereignty over land spawning dictators which in this comparison would be the kings that ruled over Europe.

Such dictatorships would enable safety and consequently economic growth as can be seen in China or Turkey ( http://www.theguardian.com/world/2014/jan/09/turkey-instability-threatens-economic-success-erdogan ) and even in Egypt (and in fact many other middle-eastern countries), which inspired by the West sought democracy failed and ended up with new dictatorships with its people being happy for it. It depends what you mean by 'best'. What you're really asking here is a valuation question something like this: "what features of a government do you value personally?"

Imagine a pure democracy. Everyone would have an equal say, a fact that many people would call intrinsically beneficial. But if every single spoke equally loudly about every single issue, it would be really hard to actually make decisions--and you'd have a ton of uneducated people with the same power as the highest-educated.

In a pure technocracy, on the other hand, average citizens would be totally disenfranchised, a fact that many people (including me!) would find troubling. But of course you'd have only the best-educated, most disinterested people making the calls, which would almost certainly lead to some good consequences.

But, getting back to your question, it's not clear that one of those options is actually better than the other. So what you really want to know is what we value in our government.

Ultimately these normative questions would have to be grounded upon an ethical theory whereby each slight difference does become differentiable in the extent to which they are better. The application of a pure democracy and a pure technocracy on two exactly similar societies would have varying results, making either one better based upon what ethical theory you hold.
I think we probably agree on the basic point there--I'd just say that it's about individual valuation. We don't need broad ethical theories for that.

From a pure standpoint, I would say a benevolent dictatorship would be the best for getting things done, and for helping out the population.
